steps.title: Germany and Europe
steps.body: Germany grows about 40% of the world's Riesling, in the Mosel, Rheingau, Pfalz, Nahe and Rheinhessen. Alsace makes dry, fuller Riesling. Austria's Wachau, Kamptal and Kremstal make dry, powerful versions on steep terraces. It's also grown in northern Italy and across central Europe.

steps.title: The New World
steps.body: Australia's Clare and Eden Valleys make dry, lime-scented Riesling that ages toward toast. New Zealand's Marlborough and Central Otago, Washington State, New York's Finger Lakes and Canada's Niagara also excel. Riesling needs cool or moderate climates to keep its acidity and aromas.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Riesling style.
steps.explanation: Each region gives Riesling a different accent.

steps.title: Site expression
steps.body: Because Riesling is unoaked and unblended, it shows soil and site clearly. Slate gives smoky, delicate wines; volcanic soils give spice; limestone gives tension; loess gives roundness. That's why Germany and Alsace name single vineyards on labels, like Burgundy.

steps.prompt: What share of the world's Riesling does Germany grow?
steps.explanation: Germany is by far the largest producer.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Germany grows about 40% of the world's Riesling
Australia, Austria, Alsace and North America also excel
Riesling shows soil and site with unusual clarity
